method: State income tax is an estimate of the tax for the year on these wages, spread evenly over the paychecks. It is not a withholding-table lookup and not a full resident return. Each state's own standard deduction, exemptions or credits, and rate schedule for the filing status are applied, together with the state-specific rules described in that state's notes.
reciprocityNote: Reciprocity agreements generally let a resident pay income tax to the home state instead of the work state, after filing the right certificate with the employer. This estimate does not compute two state returns or a credit for taxes paid to another state. It taxes the state you select.

states.name: Alabama
states.why: Alabama taxes income at 2%, 4% and 5% after a standard deduction that shrinks as income rises, a personal exemption, and a deduction for the federal income tax you pay.
states.notes: The standard deduction follows the Department of Revenue chart: the full amount up to $25,999 of Alabama AGI, stepping down to the minimum at $35,500 ($17,750 married filing separately). The dependent exemption is $1,000 per dependent at AGI up to $50,000, $500 up to $100,000 and $300 above. Federal income tax is deductible; this estimate deducts the federal income tax it calculates for the same wages. Act 2026-604 lets workers deduct up to $1,000 of overtime premium pay for 2026 through 2028; it is applied when overtime hours are entered. Head of family uses the single rate schedule with a $5,200 maximum deduction and a $3,000 exemption.

sources.name: Alabama Department of Revenue, standard deduction chart
Alabama Department of Revenue, Overtime Premium Deduction (Act 2026-604)
Alabama Department of Revenue, withholding tax tables and instructions

The dependent credit is $125 for each dependent under 17 from 2026 ($25 for older dependents); this estimate uses $125 for every dependent entered. states.notes: Figures are the Department of Finance and Administration withholding formula effective January 1, 2026: no tax under $5,600 of net taxable income, then 2%, 3%, 3.4% and 3.7% above $26,400. states.name: Colorado
states.why: Colorado taxes federal taxable income at a flat 4.4%. Paid family and medical leave (FAMLI) is a separate paycheck line.
states.notes: Colorado starts from federal taxable income, so the federal standard deduction applies. Taxpayers with adjusted gross income above $300,000 must add back the part of their federal deduction above $12,000 ($16,000 joint). Colorado requires overtime deducted on the federal return to be added back, so the federal overtime deduction does not reduce Colorado tax. Colorado starts from federal taxable income, so the federal deduction for tips also comes off Colorado taxable income. From 2026 Colorado adds the overtime deduction back (House Bill 25-1296), so overtime is taxed in full.

states.why: Vermont taxes income at 3.35%, 6.6%, 7.6% and 8.75% after its standard deduction and a $5,400 exemption per person.
states.notes: 2026 bracket thresholds and the $5,400 exemption match the Department of Taxes' 2026 withholding tables. The 2026 standard deduction ($7,850 single, $15,700 joint, $11,750 head of household) is the 2025 amount raised by the same inflation factor, because the Department's 2026 rate schedule had not been found when this was checked. Head of household is estimated on the single schedule, which runs slightly high.

sources.name: USDA National Finance Center, Vermont withholding formula, 2026
Vermont Department of Taxes, individuals

states.name: Virginia
states.why: Virginia taxes income at 2% to 5.75% (the top rate starts at $17,000) after an $8,750 standard deduction ($17,500 joint) and a $930 exemption per person.
states.notes: The standard deduction is $8,750 single and $17,500 joint for 2025 and 2026.

states.name: Washington
states.why: Washington does not tax wages. Paid family and medical leave and the WA Cares long-term care premium are paycheck lines.

states.name: West Virginia
states.why: West Virginia taxes income at five rates from 2.11% to 4.58% for 2026 after a $2,000 exemption per person.
states.notes: Senate Bill 392 (signed March 31, 2026) cut every rate by about 5%, retroactive to January 1, 2026; the top rate is now 4.58%. Joint filers use the same brackets as single filers. West Virginia has no standard deduction.

states.name: Wisconsin
states.why: Wisconsin taxes income at 3.5%, 4.4%, 5.3% and 7.65% after a standard deduction that shrinks as income rises and a $700 exemption per person.
states.notes: 2026 rate schedules and the sliding standard deduction are from the Department of Revenue's 2026 Form 1-ES instructions. A single filer's deduction is $13,960 up to $20,119 of income, falls by 12% of income above $20,120 and is gone at $136,453; joint filers start at $25,840 and lose 19.778% of income above $29,040.

sources.name: Wisconsin Department of Revenue, 2026 Form 1-ES instructions

states.changed: The sliding standard deduction is now calculated (the full deduction was being given at every income); head-of-household deduction and separate schedule added.

states.name: District of Columbia
states.why: The District of Columbia taxes income at seven rates from 4% to 10.75% after the federal standard deduction.
states.notes: D.C. uses the federal standard deduction amounts. Paid family leave in D.C. is paid by employers, not withheld from employees.
